title.zh: 第一部分 - 预订酒店房间

sections.passage: A phone conversation between a business traveller, Mr. Chen, and a reservations clerk at the Grandview Hotel. Mr. Chen needs to book accommodation for a three-night business trip. The clerk, Rebecca, asks about his preferred dates, and Mr. Chen explains that he will be arriving on Monday the 17th of March and departing on Thursday the 20th. Rebecca checks availability and offers three room types: a standard single room at 95 pounds per night, a deluxe double room at 145 pounds per night, and a business suite at 210 pounds per night. The business suite includes a separate sitting area with a work desk, complimentary high-speed internet, and access to the executive lounge, which serves free breakfast and evening drinks. Mr. Chen opts for the business suite since he will be working in the room during the evenings. Rebecca asks about his payment method, and Mr. Chen provides his company credit card details. She also asks whether he requires airport transfers, and Mr. Chen says he would like to book a taxi from the airport, which the hotel can arrange for a flat fee of 35 pounds. Rebecca confirms that the hotel has a fitness centre open from 6 AM to 10 PM, a restaurant called The Terrace that serves dinner from 6:30 to 9:30 PM, and a concierge service that can help with restaurant reservations and theatre tickets. Mr. Chen asks about the cancellation policy, and Rebecca explains that cancellations made more than 48 hours before the check-in date are free of charge, but late cancellations incur a fee equivalent to one night's stay. She provides a confirmation number and sends a booking confirmation email.

title.en: Section 2 - Tour of a Wildlife Sanctuary
title.zh: 第二部分 - 野生动物保护区参观

sections.passage: Welcome to Thornbury Wildlife Sanctuary. My name is Angela, and I'll be guiding you through our facility today. Thornbury was established in 1985 as a rescue centre for injured and orphaned native wildlife, and over the past thirty-eight years, we have cared for more than 45,000 animals. Our mission is threefold: to rescue and rehabilitate injured wildlife, to conduct conservation research, and to educate the public about the importance of protecting native species. The sanctuary covers 120 hectares of mixed habitat including woodland, wetland, and meadow, and is home to over 200 species of birds, mammals, and reptiles. Our most popular residents include a family of red foxes, a pair of European otters, and Bertie, our one-eyed barn owl who has become something of a local celebrity. Today's tour will take you along the Green Trail, which is approximately two kilometres long and should take about seventy-five minutes at a comfortable pace. The trail is wheelchair accessible for the first kilometre, and there are benches at regular intervals. Please stay on the marked paths and do not feed or touch the animals, as many of them are in the final stages of rehabilitation before release back into the wild. The sanctuary is open to visitors from 9 AM to 5 PM daily, with the last entry at 3:30 PM. Admission is 8 pounds for adults, 5 pounds for children aged five to fifteen, and free for under-fives. Family tickets for two adults and up to three children cost 22 pounds, which represents a saving of 6 pounds. We also offer annual membership at 45 pounds for adults, which includes unlimited visits, a quarterly newsletter, and invitations to special events such as our annual bat night walk and dawn chorus breakfast. The sanctuary gift shop sells a range of wildlife-themed merchandise, with all profits going directly to fund our rescue operations. We have a picnic area near the visitor centre, but please note that barbecues and open fires are strictly prohibited due to fire risk.

title.zh: 第三部分 - 小组作业讨论

sections.passage: Three students — Emma, Raj, and Sophie — are meeting in the university cafeteria to discuss their upcoming group assignment for their Marketing module. The assignment requires them to develop a marketing strategy for a new product launch. They have decided to focus on a hypothetical new brand of plant-based protein snack aimed at health-conscious consumers aged 18 to 35. Emma has conducted preliminary market research using online surveys and found that 72 percent of respondents in their target demographic said they would consider buying a plant-based snack if it tasted good and was priced competitively. The most important factors for consumers were taste, followed by nutritional content, then price, and finally environmental credentials. Raj has been researching competitor products and has identified three main competitors in the plant-based snack market. He notes that the market has grown by 15 percent annually over the past three years and is projected to reach 7.2 billion dollars globally by 2027. Sophie has been working on the branding and packaging design. She proposes calling the product GreenFuel and using minimalist packaging with earth tones and bold typography to appeal to the target demographic. The group discusses their marketing mix. For the product strategy, they agree on a range of five flavours sold in 50-gram individual packs and 200-gram sharing packs. For pricing, they suggest a premium positioning at 1.99 pounds for individual packs, which Raj's research shows is slightly above the market average but justified by the product's superior ingredients. For distribution, they recommend starting with online sales through the company's own website and Amazon, followed by selective retail partnerships with health food stores and gyms. For promotion, they plan to suggest a social media marketing campaign focusing on Instagram and TikTok, influencer partnerships with fitness and wellness content creators, and free sampling at university campuses and sporting events. They agree to divide the writing: Emma will write the market research section, Raj will cover competitor analysis and pricing, and Sophie will handle branding and promotion. The assignment is due on the 28th of March and must be 4,000 words plus appendices. They plan to combine their sections by the 22nd and use the remaining days for editing and formatting.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于洋流的讲座

sections.passage:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture examines the role of ocean currents in regulating the Earth's climate system. Ocean currents are continuous movements of seawater driven by a combination of wind, water density differences, the Earth's rotation, and tidal forces. These currents function as a massive conveyor belt, transporting heat, nutrients, and dissolved gases around the planet and profoundly influencing weather patterns, marine ecosystems, and human civilisation. The most significant ocean current system is the thermohaline circulation, often called the global ocean conveyor belt. This system is driven by differences in water temperature and salinity, which together determine water density. In the North Atlantic, warm surface water carried northward by the Gulf Stream releases heat into the atmosphere, warming Western Europe by several degrees above what would otherwise be expected at its latitude. As this water cools and becomes saltier through evaporation and ice formation, it becomes denser and sinks to the deep ocean in a process known as deep water formation. The primary sites for this process are the Nordic Seas and the Labrador Sea. The cold, dense water then flows southward along the ocean floor, eventually reaching the Southern Ocean, where it is redistributed to the Indian and Pacific Oceans before eventually resurfacing and completing a cycle that takes approximately one thousand years.

The Gulf Stream is perhaps the most well-known ocean current. It originates in the Gulf of Mexico, flows through the Straits of Florida, and then travels northward along the eastern coast of North America before crossing the Atlantic towards Europe. At its peak, the Gulf Stream transports approximately 30 million cubic metres of water per second, which is roughly one hundred times the flow of the Amazon River. This immense river of warm water has a profound effect on the climate of northwestern Europe, keeping the British Isles and Scandinavia significantly warmer than other regions at similar latitudes, such as Newfoundland and Labrador in Canada.

In the Pacific Ocean, the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, commonly known as El Nino, represents one of the most important climate phenomena on Earth. Under normal conditions, trade winds blow from east to west across the tropical Pacific, pushing warm surface water towards Southeast Asia and Australia and allowing cold, nutrient-rich water to upwell along the coast of South America. Every two to seven years, these trade winds weaken or reverse, allowing the warm water to spread eastward. This phenomenon, known as El Nino, disrupts weather patterns globally, causing droughts in Australia and Southeast Asia, heavy rainfall and flooding in South America, and altered weather patterns across North America. Its counterpart, La Nina, is characterised by stronger-than-normal trade winds and intensified normal conditions, often bringing opposite effects. The most recent major El Nino event in 2015 to 2016 was one of the strongest on record and caused an estimated 60 billion dollars in economic damages worldwide.

Climate change poses significant risks to ocean current systems. Research published in the journal Nature in 2021 suggested that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, of which the Gulf Stream is a part, has weakened by approximately 15 percent since the mid-20th century. The primary cause appears to be the influx of freshwater from the melting Greenland ice sheet, which reduces the salinity and density of North Atlantic surface water, inhibiting the sinking process that drives the circulation. Some climate models suggest that if global warming continues unchecked, the AMOC could weaken by a further 34 to 45 percent by 2100, with potentially catastrophic consequences for European agriculture, weather patterns, and marine ecosystems. While a complete collapse of the AMOC remains unlikely in the near term, even a significant weakening could shift tropical rain belts, intensify droughts in Africa, and accelerate sea-level rise along the eastern coast of North America. Understanding and monitoring these vital ocean systems is therefore essential for predicting and preparing for the impacts of climate change.

sections.passage:
Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water, with an estimated three billion cups consumed daily. Its origins trace back nearly 5,000 years to ancient China, where, according to legend, the Emperor Shen Nung discovered tea in 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tea tree blew into his pot of boiling water. While this story is almost certainly apocryphal, archaeological evidence confirms that tea was consumed in China's Yunnan province as early as the 2nd century BC, initially as a medicinal drink.

During the Tang Dynasty, tea drinking became a refined cultural practice. The scholar Lu Yu wrote The Classic of Tea, the first known monograph on tea cultivation and preparation, around 760 AD. His work codified the art of tea and elevated it from a simple beverage to a spiritual practice. Tea was prepared by boiling compressed tea cakes, and the beverage spread from China to Japan via Buddhist monks in the early 9th century. In Japan, tea drinking evolved into the highly formalised tea ceremony, or chanoyu, which embodies principles of harmony, respect, purity, and tranquillity that remain central to Japanese culture.

Tea reached Europe in the early 17th century through Portuguese and Dutch traders. The Dutch East India Company began importing tea to Europe in 1610, and it quickly became fashionable among the European aristocracy. In Britain, tea was initially an expensive luxury affordable only by the wealthy, but its popularity grew rapidly. The British East India Company monopolised the tea trade, importing vast quantities from China. By the mid-18th century, tea had become Britain's national drink, and tea consumption had profound social and economic consequences. The British government's taxation of tea led to smuggling on a massive scale and contributed to political unrest, most notably the Boston Tea Party of 1773, which helped trigger the American War of Independence.

Britain's desire to break China's monopoly on tea production led to one of the most significant acts of industrial espionage in history. In the 1840s, Scottish botanist Robert Fortune was sent by the East India Company to China to steal tea plants and learn the secrets of tea cultivation and processing. Disguised as a Chinese merchant, Fortune travelled through tea-growing regions, collecting plants, seeds, and detailed knowledge of production techniques. He successfully smuggled thousands of tea plants and a team of Chinese tea workers to British India, where they established the tea industry in Assam and Darjeeling. Within decades, India surpassed China as the world's largest tea producer, a position it held until recently.

Today, tea production is a major global industry worth over 50 billion dollars annually. The four largest tea-producing countries are China, India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka, which together account for approximately 75 percent of global production. The industry provides livelihoods for millions of smallholder farmers, particularly in developing countries. However, the tea industry faces significant challenges, including the effects of climate change on growing conditions, labour rights concerns on tea estates, and competition from other beverages. The speciality tea market, including premium loose-leaf teas and artisanal blends, has grown significantly as consumers increasingly seek higher quality and more diverse tea experiences. The future of the industry will likely depend on its ability to balance mass-market production with sustainable practices and premium offerings.

sections.passage:
Memory is the faculty by which the brain encodes, stores, and retrieves information. It is fundamental to virtually every aspect of human cognition and behaviour, from recognising a friend's face to mastering a musical instrument. Understanding how memory works — and why it sometimes fails — has been one of the central pursuits of cognitive psychology and neuroscience, with profound implications for education, clinical medicine, and our understanding of what it means to be human.

The most widely accepted model of memory distinguishes between three main stages. Sensory memory is the briefest form, lasting only milliseconds to seconds, and acts as a buffer for incoming sensory information. Short-term memory, also called working memory, can hold approximately seven items (plus or minus two) for about twenty to thirty seconds without rehearsal. Long-term memory has essentially unlimited capacity and can store information for a lifetime. The process of moving information from short-term to long-term memory is called consolidation, and it is during this process that sleep plays a critical role. Research has shown that the brain replays and strengthens newly formed memories during slow-wave sleep, transferring them from the hippocampus — a seahorse-shaped structure critical for forming new memories — to the neocortex for permanent storage.

Not all memories are created equal. Episodic memory refers to personal experiences and events — your memory of your first day at school, for example. Semantic memory stores general knowledge and facts, such as knowing that Paris is the capital of France. Procedural memory involves skills and habits, like riding a bicycle or typing on a keyboard. These different types of memory are processed by different brain systems, which is why a person with amnesia might lose the ability to form new episodic memories while retaining their procedural skills.

Psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus pioneered the scientific study of memory in the 1880s with his experiments on nonsense syllables. His most enduring contribution was the discovery of the forgetting curve, which demonstrates that memory loss follows a predictable pattern: we forget approximately 50 percent of new information within the first hour of learning it, and about 70 percent within 24 hours, unless we actively review the material. This finding has important implications for educational practice, suggesting that spaced repetition — reviewing material at gradually increasing intervals — is far more effective than massed practice, commonly known as cramming.

More recent research has identified several evidence-based strategies for improving learning and retention. The testing effect, also known as retrieval practice, has been shown to be one of the most powerful learning techniques. Rather than simply re-reading notes, students who test themselves on the material — by answering practice questions, for example — retain significantly more information over time. Elaborative interrogation, which involves asking 'why' questions about new material and connecting it to existing knowledge, also enhances retention. Interleaving — mixing different topics or types of problems during study sessions — has been shown to improve the ability to discriminate between concepts and apply knowledge flexibly, even though it feels more difficult than practising one type of problem at a time.

The malleability of memory is perhaps its most surprising and concerning feature. Research by Elizabeth Loftus and others has demonstrated that memories can be altered, distorted, or even entirely fabricated by post-event information, suggestion, and imagination. In a famous series of experiments, Loftus showed that asking participants 'How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?' rather than '...when they hit each other?' significantly altered their speed estimates and even led some participants to 'remember' seeing broken glass that was never there. This research has profound implications for the legal system, particularly regarding the reliability of eyewitness testimony, and has contributed to the reform of police interview procedures in many countries.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Future of Space Exploration
title.zh: 文章3 - 太空探索的未来

sections.passage:
Humanity stands at a pivotal moment in the history of space exploration. Fifty years after the Apollo Moon landings, a new era of space activity is unfolding, driven by a combination of technological advances, commercial investment, and renewed governmental ambition. Unlike the Cold War-era space race, which was primarily a competition between two superpowers, today's space exploration landscape involves a diverse array of national space agencies, private companies, and international partnerships, all pursuing goals ranging from lunar colonisation to Mars exploration to asteroid mining.

The commercialisation of space has been one of the most transformative developments of the 21st century. Companies such as SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab have dramatically reduced the cost of reaching orbit by developing reusable rocket technology. SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket, which can land its first stage booster for refurbishment and relaunch, has reduced the cost per kilogram of payload to low Earth orbit from approximately 54,500 dollars on the Space Shuttle to around 2,720 dollars — a reduction of roughly 95 percent. This cost reduction has opened space to a much wider range of actors, from telecommunications companies deploying satellite constellations to developing nations launching their first satellites.

NASA's Artemis programme represents the United States' commitment to returning humans to the Moon. Named after the twin sister of Apollo in Greek mythology, the programme aims to land the first woman and the first person of colour on the lunar surface and establish a sustainable human presence there. The Artemis architecture includes the Space Launch System, the most powerful rocket ever built, the Orion crew capsule, and the Gateway, a small space station that will orbit the Moon and serve as a staging point for lunar surface missions. NASA plans to use the Moon as a proving ground for the technologies and operational experience needed for the much more ambitious goal of sending humans to Mars.

The prospect of a crewed mission to Mars has captured the imagination of scientists and the public alike, but the technical challenges are formidable. A one-way trip to Mars takes approximately six to nine months, during which astronauts would be exposed to dangerous levels of cosmic radiation, experience significant muscle and bone loss due to prolonged weightlessness, and face the psychological challenges of extreme isolation. The total mission duration, including surface operations and the return journey, would be approximately two to three years. SpaceX founder Elon Musk has announced plans for a crewed Mars mission using the Starship vehicle, with aspirational timelines targeting the late 2020s, though most experts consider the 2030s a more realistic timeframe for such a mission.

Beyond exploration, space offers significant economic potential. The global space economy was valued at approximately 469 billion dollars in 2023, encompassing satellite communications, Earth observation, navigation services, and space tourism. Asteroid mining, while still in its conceptual stages, could potentially provide access to vast quantities of rare metals and minerals. A single metallic asteroid just 500 metres in diameter could contain more platinum-group metals than have ever been mined on Earth. However, the legal framework governing space resources remains underdeveloped. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which forms the foundation of international space law, declares that space is the 'province of all mankind' and prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies, but its provisions regarding resource extraction are ambiguous and subject to competing interpretations.

Space debris represents one of the most pressing challenges facing the space industry. There are currently over 36,000 objects larger than ten centimetres orbiting the Earth, along with an estimated one million objects between one and ten centimetres, and over 130 million smaller fragments. Even tiny pieces of debris can cause catastrophic damage to spacecraft due to the extreme velocities involved — orbital speeds typically exceed 28,000 kilometres per hour. The risk of a cascading chain reaction of collisions, known as the Kessler Syndrome, could eventually render certain orbital regimes unusable. Several organisations are developing active debris removal technologies, including robotic arms, nets, and harpoons, while regulatory measures such as mandatory deorbiting of defunct satellites within five years of end of life are being implemented. The long-term sustainability of space activities depends on addressing this growing problem before it becomes unmanageable.
